shared_context.patient: A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain. He first felt the pain while lifting boxes at work but thought that he had just strained a muscle. The pain appears to be worse in the mornings and after rest. Exercise and physical activity appear to temporarily make the pain better. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen for the pain. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he is found to have limited flexion and extension of his spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of his patellar tendons bilaterally. Results from laboratory tests are shown below: Serum: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 61 mm/hr C-reactive protein (CRP): 36 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L)

snippets.output: The pain worsens after rest, which suggests inflammatory back pain.
snippets.pattern_notes: Isolated false atom kept separate from true claims.

snippets.output: The patient has tenderness over the insertion of the patellar tendons bilaterally, which suggests enthesitis.
The combination of chronic back pain, morning stiffness, improvement with activity, and enthesitis suggests a spondyloarthropathy, such as ankylosing spondylitis (AS).
snippets.notes: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is just an item after “such as,” not an only possibility; this decomposition destroys the “such as” relationship.

snippets.output: Bone Scan: Not typically used for the initial diagnosis of spondyloarthropathies.

snippets.output: Computed Tomography (CT): Useful for detecting bony changes.
CT is less sensitive than Magnetic MRI for early inflammatory changes.

snippets.output: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Highly sensitive for detecting early inflammatory changes.
